title: Why Are Indian Children So Short? The Role of Birth Order and Son Preference
research_question: Why are Indian children, on average, so much shorter than children in poorer regions such as sub-Saharan Africa? Specifically, to what extent does parental favoritism toward eldest sons—operating through fertility decisions and the allocation of health and nutrition resources across siblings—explain India's high rate of child stunting and its steep decline in child height with birth order?
data_description: The primary dataset is the 2005–2006 Indian National Family Health Survey (NFHS-3), combined with Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS) from 25 sub-Saharan African countries surveyed between 2004 and 2010, yielding anthropometric data on over 168,000 children aged 0–5. The unit of observation is a child. Key outcomes include height-for-age z-scores, weight-for-age z-scores, stunting status, hemoglobin levels, and infant mortality. Health input variables cover prenatal care visits, iron supplementation, tetanus shots, facility delivery, postnatal checkups, child iron pills, and vaccinations. Controls include maternal age, literacy, height, child age in months, and primary sampling unit. Within-India analyses additionally use pooled NFHS waves (1992–93, 1998–99, 2005–06) covering over 90,000 children and the Indian Human Development Survey (IHDS) panel (2005 and 2012), which permits identification of mothers with completed fertility.
institutional_context: India has the world's highest concentration of stunted children, with stunting rates above 40 percent—exceeding those in much poorer sub-Saharan African countries despite India's higher income and better performance on other health indicators. The setting is shaped by Hindu kinship norms that are patrilocal and patrilineal: aging parents typically reside with and bequeath property to their eldest son, and Hindu religious texts emphasize post-death rituals requiring a male heir. This generates strong eldest-son preference, distinct from general son preference, influencing how parents allocate food, health care, and prenatal/postnatal investments across siblings, and shaping fertility-stopping behavior whereby families lacking a son continue childbearing beyond their desired family size. Variation in these norms exists across Indian regions (e.g., matrilineal practices in Kerala and Northeastern states), across child sex ratios, and across religious groups (Hindu versus Muslim), as well as relative to neighboring Bangladesh and Pakistan.

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.identification_strategy: EVENT STUDY — treatment = later-born children, control = first-born children; shock/instrument/cutoff = birth order and son preference
_legacy_v1_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: The study finds that birth order and son preference significantly reduce the height of Indian children. Later-born children, especially girls in families that have not yet had a son, are substantially shorter due to son-preferring resource allocation. This differential investment explains much of India's height disadvantage relative to Sub-Saharan Africa.
_legacy_v1_ground_truth.main_effect: Later-born girls in families without a prior son are ~0.3–0.4 SD shorter in height-for-age z-scores
